entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (ELCA) is the largest Lutheran denomination in the United States, formed in 1988 from the merger of three Lutheran bodies and now counting approximately 3 million members. The ELCA is among the most progressive major Protestant denominations in the US, ordaining women since its founding, ordaining openly gay clergy since 2009, and blessing same-sex marriages since 2010.

Lutheranism traces its origin to Martin Luther's 1517 Ninety-Five Theses challenging Catholic indulgences, which sparked the Protestant Reformation. German and Scandinavian immigrants brought Lutheranism to America in large numbers in the 19th and early 20th centuries, creating the three predecessor bodies that merged to form the ELCA. The 1988 merger created a denomination explicitly committed to inclusivity in contrast to the more conservative Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod.

The ELCA's 2009 decision to ordain openly gay clergy in committed relationships was one of the most significant Protestant denominational decisions of the early 21st century, leading 900 of its 10,500 congregations to leave for more conservative denominations. The ELCA's Bishop Elizabeth Eaton and its predecessor Presiding Bishop Mark Hanson have been active voices on climate change, immigration reform, and racial justice. The ELCA's Lutheran World Federation membership connects it to 148 churches worldwide with 78 million adherents.
